summary: At just 1.7 square miles and roughly 1,740 residents, Hidden Hills is a gated equestrian community in the western San Fernando Valley that functions less like a city and more like a single private neighborhood — one of the smallest incorporated municipalities in Los Angeles County, governed by its own city council yet containing no commercial district, no traffic lights, and essentially no sidewalks, replaced instead by a network of dirt horse trails that thread between properties. The median home value exceeds $2 million against a median household income above $250,000, yielding a price-to-income ratio north of 8:1 — steep even by that income tier — and the $3,500-plus median rent reflects a market where almost everything is owner-occupied on large lots. With an average daily high of 76°F and nearly ten hours of sunshine, the climate is quintessential inland Southern California: warm and dry, though summer days in this valley-edge pocket push well past that average. There is no real employment base here; this is a bedroom community whose residents commute into greater Los Angeles for work in entertainment, professional services, and other industries accessible via the 101 freeway. The single school scores impressively — ELA performance at nearly 43 points above standard, math at 30 above — but daily errands, grocery shopping, dining, and virtually all commerce require driving into neighboring Calabasas or beyond. Hidden Hills trades every conventional urban amenity for acreage, privacy, and bridle paths, which makes it less a town to evaluate on typical livability metrics and more a specific lifestyle proposition with a correspondingly specific price tag.
